question.question: Why can a single pediatric PN template not be used across all ages?
choices: Gestational age, organ maturity, growth, weight, and tolerance change requirements
Weight alone determines identical per-kilogram targets at every age
An adult PN template can be scaled by weight without assessing neonatal tolerance
Age changes the product label but has no effect on nutrient needs
question.rationale: Developmental age, organ maturity, growth, illness, and weight affect requirements and tolerance. A weight-only or scaled adult template cannot replace the pediatric assessment.

question.question: Why should enteral readiness be reassessed during PN?
choices: The gastrointestinal route may increasingly meet needs and allow PN reduction
One ordered feed proves that all intravenous nutrition can be stopped
A fixed PN regimen remains appropriate regardless of advancing enteral intake
An energy-intake percentage alone proves adequate absorption and hydration
question.rationale: Reassess gastrointestinal function and actual tolerated intake as feeding advances. PN reduction must preserve nutrition, growth, and hydration; an order or energy percentage alone does not establish readiness.

choicesReviewed.text: The gastrointestinal route may increasingly meet needs and allow PN reduction
choicesReviewed.review: Ongoing assessment of gastrointestinal function and actual intake can permit safe PN reduction.

choicesReviewed.review: An order does not prove delivery, tolerance, absorption or adequacy.

choicesReviewed.text: A fixed PN regimen remains appropriate regardless of advancing enteral intake
choicesReviewed.review: The combined regimen must be reassessed as reliable enteral intake advances.

choicesReviewed.text: An energy-intake percentage alone proves adequate absorption and hydration
choicesReviewed.review: Energy fraction alone cannot establish absorption or fluid adequacy.

question.question: Which approach correctly accounts for daily pediatric fluid intake?
choices: Count PN, medicines, carriers, flushes, blood products, and enteral intake
Count PN and enteral intake but exclude medication and carrier volumes
Count nutrition and medicines but exclude separate lipid and flush volumes
Use urine output alone as the measure of administered fluid
question.rationale: All administered fluid contributes to intake, including separate lipid, medication carriers, and flushes. Record output separately to assess balance; urine output alone cannot measure fluid delivered.

question.question: Which assessment best represents nutrition actually received?
choices: Calculate nutrients and fluid from documented PN, lipid, and oral or enteral delivery, accounting for interruptions
Use the ordered PN bag without checking infusion completion or other routes
Use delivered mL alone without the nutrient composition
Use the previous prescription as proof of current intake
question.rationale: Calculate actual energy, protein, and fluid from delivered volumes and composition across routes. Procedures, line problems, and medication incompatibilities can interrupt delivery, so prescribed amounts may exceed what the patient received.

question.question: When should pediatric PN be reduced during transition to enteral feeding?
choices: As actual tolerated intake reliably replaces intravenous nutrients while growth, absorption, hydration, and electrolytes are assessed
As soon as a feed is ordered, before confirming delivery or tolerance
At one energy-intake percentage without reviewing protein, absorption, or fluid needs
Only after catheter removal, regardless of reliable enteral intake
question.rationale: Reconcile both routes and adjust PN to the nutrients still needed. Confirm tolerance and consider absorption, growth, hydration, and electrolytes; an ordered feed or an energy percentage alone does not establish that PN can be stopped.

choicesReviewed.text: As actual tolerated intake reliably replaces intravenous nutrients while growth, absorption, hydration, and electrolytes are assessed
choicesReviewed.review: Adjust remaining intravenous nutrition after confirming actual tolerated replacement and assessing growth, absorption, hydration and electrolytes.

choicesReviewed.text: As soon as a feed is ordered, before confirming delivery or tolerance

choicesReviewed.text: Only after catheter removal, regardless of reliable enteral intake
choicesReviewed.review: Catheter removal is not a prerequisite for reducing nutrient delivery; continuing intravenous need must be assessed.

question.question: Delivered enteral energy has reached 70 percent of the assessed energy goal, but PN remains unchanged. What is the most defensible next action?
choices: Reconcile both routes and adjust PN after assessing tolerated intake, absorption, growth, and fluid and nutrient needs
Stop all PN because one energy percentage proves every requirement is met
Reduce PN by the enteral mL alone without reviewing nutrient composition or absorption
Keep the full PN prescription indefinitely despite reliable enteral replacement
question.rationale: An energy percentage alone does not establish protein, micronutrient, or fluid adequacy, nor reliable absorption. Adjust the combined plan to prevent excess delivery while preserving growth and hydration; do not automatically stop PN.

choicesReviewed.text: Reconcile both routes and adjust PN after assessing tolerated intake, absorption, growth, and fluid and nutrient needs
choicesReviewed.review: Reconcile the combined plan and remaining needs while confirming tolerance, absorption, growth and fluid adequacy.

choicesReviewed.text: Stop all PN because one energy percentage proves every requirement is met
choicesReviewed.review: The supplied70percent energy fraction cannot prove every nutrient/fluid requirement is met.

choicesReviewed.text: Reduce PN by the enteral mL alone without reviewing nutrient composition or absorption
choicesReviewed.review: Equal volumes can provide different nutrients; absorption also matters.

choicesReviewed.text: Keep the full PN prescription indefinitely despite reliable enteral replacement
choicesReviewed.review: An unchanged full PN order despite reliable replacement can provide excessive nutrition or fluid.

teachingReview.heading: Define the patient precisely
teachingReview.body: A 900 g preterm infant, a term neonate, a toddler, and a teenager do not share one default prescription. Gestational age, postmenstrual age, postnatal age, current weight, growth velocity, organ maturity, disease, and enteral exposure change nutrient demand and tolerance. Assess growth with serial measurements and a chart appropriate to the infant's maturity and age; a single weight or an adult template cannot describe the whole nutrition plan.

sources: neonatal2025 page1 and full assessment context

clauseReview.clauses: Serial growth with appropriate chart; one weight/adult template insufficient
sources: aspen2017 pediatric13A actual intake and growth goals

teachingReview.heading: Compare more than laboratory values
teachingReview.body: Monitor actual intake, output, edema, daily or clinically appropriate weight, growth velocity, head circumference and length when relevant, glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, triglycerides, liver and kidney function, acid-base status, catheter findings, and feeding tolerance. Frequency changes with age, stability, acuity, and recent order changes. Laboratory results assess tolerance and complications; they do not establish that the prescribed nutrients were delivered or that growth goals were met.

teachingReview.heading: Transition while preserving growth
teachingReview.body: Advance enteral nutrition when clinically safe and reconcile actual delivery across both routes. Reduce PN as tolerated enteral intake reliably replaces intravenous nutrients, while checking absorption, growth, hydration, electrolytes, and the full energy and protein plan. An ordered feed or one percentage of energy intake does not establish that all nutrition and fluid needs are met, especially in intestinal failure. Assess micronutrient supplementation and a monitoring plan after PN stops. Remove central access promptly once it is no longer essential; assess continuing intravenous needs before deciding that the device is unnecessary.

teachingReview.heading: Reconcile delivered nutrients across routes
teachingReview.body: Compare the prescription with what was actually infused or fed. Use the documented volume, composition, and infusion time for PN and separate lipid, and the measured oral or enteral intake. Record interruptions for procedures, line problems, and medication incompatibilities. Convert the delivered amounts to energy, protein, and fluid totals before comparing them with the assessed goals; a delivered volume alone is not a complete nutrient assessment.

teachingReview.heading: Interpret growth with fluid and developmental context
teachingReview.body: Track serial weight, length, and head circumference in neonates using an appropriate growth chart. Weight changes can reflect fluid shifts, illness, or medicines as well as nutrition. Interpret growth trends with actual nutrient intake, hydration, examination, and the clinical course; do not equate one weight increase with adequate nutrition. In the first two postnatal weeks, the neonatal assessment tool cautions against using its proposed weight-growth malnutrition indicators and gives nutrient intake a central role. Those proposed indicators have not been validated, so they require clinical judgment.
